title: Peated Indian Whisky Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: How peated Indian single malts get their smoke, why heat changes how peat develops in the cask and how to taste the difference from Scotch.
teaser: The smoke in peated Indian whisky usually arrives in imported malt. The heat it matures in is all Indian.
standfirst: Smoky whisky started in the peat bogs of Scotland. Indian distillers now make peated single malts too. The smoke usually comes from imported malt. The maturation happens in Indian heat. That combination gives a whisky with its own character.
sections: Where the smoke in whisky comes from

Peat is partly decayed plant matter that builds up in waterlogged bogs over thousands of years. Traditionally, Scottish maltings burnt it to dry germinated barley. The smoke carries compounds called phenols into the malt. Those phenols survive mashing, fermentation and distillation in part. They give whisky its smoky, medicinal or tarry notes.

Peat levels are measured in parts per million (ppm) of phenols in the malt. Lightly peated malt might sit around 5 to 15 ppm. Heavily peated malt is often 40 to 50 ppm or more. A good deal of that is lost in distillation, so the finished spirit carries far less than the malt figure suggests. Our guide to peat and smoke in whisky goes into the chemistry.
How Indian distillers get peated malt

India has little peat suitable for malting. Indian distillers making peated whisky usually buy peated malt from maltings abroad, most often in Scotland. They ship it in. Unpeated malt can come from Indian barley, much of it six row barley grown in the north. Our guide to Indian six row barley covers that side.

The distiller chooses a peating level when ordering malt. Some peated Indian single malts are made entirely from peated malt. Others blend peated and unpeated whisky to set the level of smoke they want.
Heat changes how peat develops in the cask

This is where Indian peated whisky parts ways with Scotch. In a cool Scottish warehouse, peat smoke fades slowly over the years as oak and oxidation build up around it. A 10 year old Islay malt is often more smoky than an 18 year old from the same distillery.

In Indian heat, the whole process runs faster. Warehouses can sit above 30 °C for months. Spirit moves in and out of the oak more quickly. Evaporation losses run far above Scotland's commonly quoted figure of around 2% a year. A peated Indian malt can show rich oak, vanilla and tropical fruit at four or five years, sitting alongside smoke that has not had time to fade.

That is why peated Indian whisky often tastes both young and mature at once: bright smoke with deep, sweet oak. It is a different balance from an old Scotch, not a lesser one.
Why the ppm figure can mislead

Some labels quote the peating level of the malt. It is a useful clue but not the whole story. Two distilleries using malt at the same ppm can make whisky with very different smoke.

The reason is the stills. The heavier, smokier phenols tend to come through later in the spirit run. A distiller who keeps collecting spirit later into the run, a later cut, keeps more of them. One who cuts earlier makes a cleaner, less smoky spirit from the same malt. Cask choice then adds its own layer: active first fill casks can soften smoke with sweetness, while tired refill casks let it stand out. The ppm on the malt is where the smoke starts, not where it ends.
What to expect in the glass

Peat gives different things to different noses. Common descriptors:

  • Campfire and wood smoke. Dry, ashy, like a dying bonfire.
  • Medicinal. Antiseptic, iodine, sticking plaster.
  • Tarry or rubbery. Heavier phenols, sometimes like smoked meat.
  • Sweet smoke. Smoke wrapped around vanilla and fruit, common in ex-bourbon matured peated malts.

Indian peated whiskies often lean towards sweet smoke because of the fast, heavy oak extraction in heat. Bottlings at higher strength also carry the smoke harder, so try them with a few drops of water.

Set up a small flight: a peated Indian single malt, a peated Scotch and an unpeated Indian malt. Pour 15 ml of each. Nose the unpeated one first so the smoke does not overwhelm your nose.

Ask three questions. How strong is the smoke and what kind is it? How much oak and sweetness sits behind it? Which flavours does the Indian peated malt share with its unpeated sibling? That shared layer is the distillery and the climate. The difference is the peat.

Smoke is loud. It masks subtler aromas for a beginner. Learning to look past it, to find the fruit and oak underneath, is one of the clearest signs of a trained palate.
Pairing peated whisky with Indian food

Smoky whisky can sit well with tandoori dishes, where char from the clay oven meets smoke in the glass. It can clash with delicate fish curries or very sweet desserts. Our guide to whisky and Indian food pairing has more ideas. As always, sip slowly with plenty of water. Never drink and drive.

Buy a small bottle or a single pour of a peated Indian single malt and a peated Scotch. Taste them side by side with water on hand. Write one line each on the smoke and one line on what sits under it. That second line is where the climate shows.
faqs: How do Indian distillers make peated whisky?
Most buy peated malt from maltings abroad, often in Scotland, because India has little peat suitable for malting. The whisky is then distilled and matured in India.
Is peated Indian whisky as smoky as Islay Scotch?
It depends on the peating level the distiller chooses. Heat speeds maturation, so Indian peated malts often pair bright smoke with rich oak at a young age.
What does ppm mean for peated whisky?
It is parts per million of phenols in the malt, a measure of how heavily the barley was peated. Much of it is lost in distillation.
